[RESPONSE] My main concern is worsening difficulty walking — it started about three months ago and has progressed to the point that I’ve needed a wheelchair for the last month.

[THOUGHT] Rapidly progressive gait disturbance leading to wheelchair dependence over months raises concern for spinal cord myelopathy (compressive or inflammatory), peripheral neuropathy, neuromuscular disease, or central causes. Presence of new bladder or bowel dysfunction would strongly support spinal cord involvement and prioritize urgent imaging. I need that single critical piece next.

[QUERY] Have you developed any new problems with bladder or bowel control (incontinence, difficulty urinating, urinary urgency or retention, or new constipation) since your walking difficulty began?

[REFERENCE] 2. The patient has been experiencing a gradual difficulty in walking over the past 3 months.
4. There is a history of urinary incontinence for 1 year.

[RESPONSE] I have had urinary incontinence for 1 year, and my walking difficulty began 3 months ago — so the urinary incontinence did not develop since the walking difficulty started.

[THOUGHT] Age is a fundamental piece of information that strongly influences the differential (e.g., normal-pressure hydrocephalus in older adults, demyelinating disease in younger adults, metastatic disease in older patients). I have not yet asked this, so I must obtain it before ordering specific exams or imaging.

[QUERY] How old are you?

[THOUGHT] Urinary incontinence preceded gait decline, which raises possibilities including normal-pressure hydrocephalus (gait + urinary + cognitive), neurodegenerative disease, or spinal pathology with early autonomic involvement. Determining whether there are cognitive changes will help distinguish NPH from spinal or peripheral causes and guide next tests (brain imaging vs spinal MRI). I will ask one focused question about cognition.

[QUERY] Have you noticed any changes in your memory, thinking speed, attention, or personality since the urinary incontinence or walking problems began?

[REFERENCE] N/A
[RESPONSE] I don't recall any changes in my memory, thinking speed, attention, or personality.

[THOUGHT] A history of urinary incontinence for a year followed by rapidly progressive gait decline to wheelchair dependence suggests possible spinal cord myelopathy (compressive lesion such as tumor, epidural abscess, or severe degenerative stenosis). This is an urgent structural concern where imaging is the most informative next step. Rather than further history that might delay diagnosis, urgent MRI of the spine is warranted to identify cord compression and guide treatment.

[TEST] Urgent MRI of the entire spine (cervical, thoracic, and lumbar) with and without gadolinium contrast.
9. MRI Brain and Spinal Cord findings: Multiple areas of atrophy and signal changes in the brainstem, cerebellum, and basal ganglia, consistent with neurodegenerative processes.

[THOUGHT] MRI shows neurodegenerative changes in brainstem, cerebellum, and basal ganglia — pattern suggests a synucleinopathy like multiple system atrophy (MSA) or other atypical parkinsonian syndromes. Presence of parkinsonian motor signs (bradykinesia/rigidity/tremor) would support MSA-P; predominant cerebellar signs would support MSA-C. I need to know whether parkinsonian motor features are present before committing to a diagnosis.

[QUERY] Do you have slowness of movement (bradykinesia), stiffness/rigidity of your limbs, or a resting tremor?

[REFERENCE] N/A
[RESPONSE] I'm not sure — I don't recall whether I have slowness of movement, stiffness, or a resting tremor.

[THOUGHT] MRI shows neurodegenerative changes in brainstem, cerebellum, and basal ganglia with early autonomic failure (urinary incontinence) and rapidly progressive gait impairment — this strongly suggests multiple system atrophy (MSA). To distinguish MSA subtypes and strengthen the diagnosis I need one focused sign of cerebellar involvement. Asking about speech (dysarthria) is a single, high-yield question.

[QUERY] Have you developed slurred, slow, or unclear speech (dysarthria)?

[REFERENCE] 5. Recent onset of speech slurring making communication challenging.

[RESPONSE] Yes — I have recently developed slurred speech that makes communication challenging.

[THOUGHT] The patient is a 54-year-old with one year of urinary incontinence (autonomic failure), rapidly progressive gait impairment over 3 months leading to wheelchair dependence, MRI showing neurodegenerative atrophy and signal changes in brainstem, cerebellum, and basal ganglia, and recent dysarthria consistent with cerebellar dysfunction. This combination of early autonomic failure, cerebellar signs, and corresponding MRI changes makes multiple system atrophy most likely, specifically the cerebellar-predominant subtype (MSA-C).

[DIAGNOSIS] Multiple system atrophy, cerebellar predominant (MSA-C).
